speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It was titled "Strengthening Singapore's Fight Against Drugs".

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There were suggestions on how we can respond to challenges in the fight against drugs in the drug situation that we were and are facing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Several Members also made good suggestions on how we can improve our approach to rehabilitation, how we can involve families more in the rehabilitation process and how we can provide better support for abusers after they have been released.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have looked at these carefully and we have been analysing the situation and also looking at the evidence that we have been collecting in our dealings with abusers both in the Drug Rehabilitation Centres (DRCs) and post-release.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the current amendments arise from that set of factors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, these amendments to the Misuse of Drugs Act (MDA) have two primary focuses in broad categories.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They will make some additional actions offences; they will give some greater enforcement powers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The second part of it, they will give a much greater focus on rehabilitation and move away a little bit from the philosophy of long-term detentions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will make some actions, including actions which we will categorise as contamination offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is a range of contaminative behaviours that may not meet the current definition of trafficking or abetment, but they contribute to the spread of drug abuse.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, clause 3 introduces a new set of offences which targets acts of contamination.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The proposed new section 11C will make it an offence if you introduce a person to a trafficker, and if you know or have reason to believe that the person intends to procure or consume drugs and the trafficker is likely to supply them.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One example would be a student who offers to introduce friends to a trafficker to buy cannabis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The student himself does not take cannabis, did not take part in the transaction, but he facilitated his friend's drug consumption.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to try and deter such conduct.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Section 11D(1) will make it an offence if you were to teach, instruct, provide instructions to another person, on the carrying out of drug activities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They could be activities like consumption, cultivation, manufacturing, trafficking, importing and exporting, knowing or having reason to believe that the person intends to carry out such drug activity.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There will be no mandatory minimum for the first conviction.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, supposing the perpetrator has no knowledge of the recipient's intent to commit a drug activity, nevertheless, the perpetrator has still caused harm.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: He has spread information on the carrying out of drug activities.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, clause 3 will have a section 11D(2), which will make it an offence to disseminate or publish information on the carrying out of any of the drug activities – those which I mentioned earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this can cover a range of behaviour, from the irresponsible – like putting out or posting information on how to manufacture drugs, and if you were to put it up on social media where others can see it, to the downright malicious, like trying to teach and influence friends into taking drugs with one.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have to try and stop such behaviours.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If there are second or subsequent convictions, there will be a mandatory minimum sentence of one year.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When you criminalise with this framework, you need to provide a proper set of defences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Defences would include legitimate purposes, like administration of justice, science, medicine, education, art.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you did this for any purposes of any of those, then there could be exemptions.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Subsidiary legislation will set out scope of authorised activities which will not be caught by the contamination offences I just spoke about, and clause 20 provides for that.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is aimed at better protecting our children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you would look at section 11B – if an adult possesses illicit drug and then, knowingly or recklessly, leave it within the reach of a child, access of a child, that would be an offence.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If an adult permits a young person to consume drugs which are in the adult's possession, or does not take reasonable steps to prevent that from happening, that would also be an offence – the young person is under 21.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: One example: in October 2016, or two years ago, we had two young children, aged two and four; they accidentally consumed their father’s drugs, fell unconscious and they were rushed to the Accidents and Emergency (A&E) department.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At present, parents and guardians are required to attend counselling, but some parents persistently absent themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: CNB will, even after the new legislation comes into force, understand their context, try and understand why they do not want to come, and will use these powers very sparingly.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But as a last resort, if the parents and guardians refused to be involved in their children's counselling without reasonable excuse, then they can potentially be exposed to charges.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: When there is a young drug abuser, the impact is on that person, and on the rest of the society.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The parents must bear some responsibility, too, and they must come in and try and help.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The State provides the counselling, so they should come in and take the counselling and see how they can help their children.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Next, we move to hair analysis and oral fluid testing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Urine tests are able to detect only drugs that had been consumed within the week.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hair analysis goes further back; it can detect drugs which had been consumed earlier.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Hair analysis now applies to the monitoring of those under supervision.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Health Sciences Authority (HSA), in its research and science, has enhanced the effectiveness and reliability of hair analysis.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if you are tested positive on hair analysis, you can be directed for rehabilitation and supervision orders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If a person fails to provide hair specimens, then he or she will face the same punishments and liabilities as a failure to provide urine specimens.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, these persons, if they intentionally refuse to provide the required specimens for testing with no reasonable excuse, then they can face charges.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We are also introducing the use of oral fluid, saliva, to test for drug abuse.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is clause 15 of the Bill with a new section 31B.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, enforcement officers can require a suspected abuser to provide oral fluids for the purpose of testing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But the testing of oral fluids is for the purpose of immediate and effective and efficient screening of suspects, particularly in the context of a mass raid or large crowds.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Officers can then prioritise individuals who require further hair or urine testing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Oral fluid tests will be an efficient method of screening; they will not be used for prosecution or emplacement on rehabilitation or supervision.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will continue to rely on urine or hair tests for the purposes of rehabilitation orders or supervision orders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those are the aspects in which the Act is proposed to be changed in terms of increasing the powers, enforcement powers, or adding in some new offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Now, let me move on to the rehabilitation aspect of the Bill.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Drug abusers today, arrested for the first and second time, go through rehabilitation, which is mandatory, in DRCs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We call it DRC1 and DRC2, first time and second time.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is done through orders made by the Director of the CNB under section 34 of the MDA.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There is no criminal record for DRC1 and DRC2.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The Long-Term Imprisonment (LT) regime was introduced in 1998.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That targeted hardcore abusers, who, at that time, formed three-quarters or more than three-quarters of the abusers who were being arrested.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The purpose was to punish, but also to deter their drug use because everything else has been tried, but it was not possible to keep them away from drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were getting into drugs, and they were contaminating others, and the problem was spreading.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it was to protect the public from abusers who turned to crime to feed their drug habits as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, third-time abusers face mandatory imprisonment of five to seven years, and three to six strokes of the cane.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Fourth time and beyond: seven to 13 years in LT.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In LT2, six to 12 strokes of the cane.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, from the beginning of the LT regime, together with other efforts on the enforcement side as well as the rehabilitation side, the drug situation in Singapore has improved.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you can say, it is about halved, which is, as I have said in other fora, quite a remarkable record because all things are not equal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: People's ability to afford drugs has increased, the amount of drugs being produced in the region and available internationally has increased, so, all things being equal, the number of arrests should have gone up, not gone down.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, it is a testament to the way CNB has worked.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The entire framework has worked to help our people keep off drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Education, prevention, a strong enforcement, an efficient CNB, an efficient legal framework – all have worked together.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And the strong support that has been given, both in this House and outside, by the public, for the stand we have taken.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: At the same time, over these years, Singapore Prison Service (SPS) and the Singapore Corporation of Rehabilitative Enterprises (SCORE) have stepped up support for abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They include high-intensity psychology-based programmes, especially for those with a higher risk of reoffending.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They were also given skills training and work programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 2014, we introduced the Mandatory Aftercare Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we target the higher-risk offenders, and they will be given compulsory structured programmes even after they are released.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: After their release is when they are at the highest risk.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Throughout this period, the evidence that we have been collecting, we have been studying how to bring down recidivism down even further.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our assessment is that, for pure abusers, we can now afford to shift our balance quite decisively and focus more on rehabilitation as opposed to detention.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We all know that long periods of detention can affect the abusers' employability after they are released.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They are in for seven years, or 12 years or 13 years; when they come out, their ability to reintegrate back into society, their ability to hold down a job, there is a lesser ability.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, really, the question is, how do you strike the balance?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What is the risk of allowing them into the community without long-term detention versus the consequences of keeping them in long-term detention?

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In 1998, we said, looking at the numbers and the way the problem was going, we have to go for long term, and one or two other number of significant factors then, too.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Today, looking at the numbers and the profile of detainees, and looking at how we are managing, we think we can afford to take the risk and let them out from DRC into society faster, without going the long-term detention route.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The answer as to where you strike the balance depends on a variety of external factors.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our view is that the situation has now changed compared to 1998.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Our two-year recidivism rates for LT inmates are encouraging.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: What that means is that within five years of their release, six out of 10 of the LT inmates will be back in prison.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Staying clean is ultimately dependent on a variety of factors, including the resolve of the abuser.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But it is a difficult journey for the abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Often, they become estranged from their families, communities and the workplace.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: It is harder for them to reintegrate once released.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A number get back into bad company, on drugs, and then they get re-arrested at various points; the cycle repeats itself over and over again.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we have decided, let us try and distinguish between those who only consume drugs – I call them the "pure" abusers – and those who also face charges for other offences, for example, trafficking, property offences, violent offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, if they have abused drugs and they have committed some of these other crimes, we put them in one category.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We put those who only abused drugs in one category.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For the second group, those who consume drugs and commit other offences, they will continue to be charged for their drug-consumption offences as well as the other offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they are liable, they will be sentenced to LT.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: For those who only abuse but do not have any other criminal offence, that means they only consume drugs and they admit to their drug abuse, then the general approach, regardless the number of times, would be that the Director of CNB will make the appropriate supervision or detention order, and channel them into the rehabilitation regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, this group of abusers may also include those who have minor consumption-related offences like possession of drug-taking utensils or possession of small quantities of drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the Attorney-General's Chambers (AGC) agrees with CNB that there is no need to charge the drug abusers for these minor offences, then these persons will also be channelled to the rehabilitation regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This will be conditional on the abusers admitting to their drug offences.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they deny their drug abuse despite the evidence, that means they have really not accepted the need for rehabilitation, they are likely to be charged in Court, if AGC concurs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: These changes, as Members will appreciate, are quite significant.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That means one out of every two for those who are going into LT could now go into a pure DRC regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And, really, to benefit as many persons as possible, CNB, with the concurrence of AGC, will generally not charge abusers who meet the criteria I have explained, from tomorrow, 16 January 2019, on the assumption that the Bill is passed today.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We also want drug abusers to come forward voluntarily for rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, moving forward, drug abusers who voluntarily submit themselves to CNB will be considered for a shorter detention in DRC.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will do a risk analysis but, based on that, they can and will be considered for shorter detention.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The abuser will still need to undergo operational and risk assessment before he or she can be considered for this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: All abusers will be given two surrender opportunities in their lifetime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now highlight the key features of this enhanced rehabilitation regime.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: In general, first-time drug abusers assessed to be of low risk of further abuse, will be put on the Enhanced Direct Supervision Order (EDSO).

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That is a non-custodial supervision order with compulsory counselling.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A case manager will provide dedicated support to these persons and their families.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Higher-risk first-time abusers, as well as repeat abusers, will undergo intensive, mandatory rehabilitation in the DRC, because that is a secure environment run by the Prisons.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The interventions will be based on their assessed risk and needs of the abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, in order to correct it, you need to target the underlying attitudes and drug addiction issues.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Second, we will also run family programmes, so that, in a sense, they will be taught how to have better relationships with their loved ones.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Because, by and large, a significant number would have very strained relationships.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We will also give them skills training and employment assistance.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is to improve their employability upon release.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Third-time and subsequent drug abusers, the Prisons will be introducing DRC3 and DRC4.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The periods will be longer than DRC1 and DRC2.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: That will apply to high-risk repeat drug abusers who are going to require a longer period of rehabilitation.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those who are assessed to be ready to be discharged from DRC to move into Community-Based Programmes (CBP), they will be put into a halfway house, or a day release scheme from a community supervision centre.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Or they could be allowed to go home with electronic tagging.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, from DRC, released into CBP, where you could be leaving in the morning, going and doing your work, coming back at night, really to keep you in as safe an environment as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Last week, I just opened the first Prisons-run halfway house.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: There are other halfway houses, so we work with partners and we financially support them as well.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, after CBP will be the supervision phase.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: During this phase, the abusers – ex-abusers, hopefully – will be required to report regularly to CNB for urine and hair testing.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Prisons, SCORE and CNB will also work with community partners.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: This is to try and help the abusers in areas, such as job training and support, casework, counselling and befriending.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have been devoting a lot of resources to the post-release support and that is why we feel confident that we can move ahead with this.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The risk of recidivism is highest in the first two years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I have given Members the figures for five years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If they can be clean for five years, then the recidivism rates drop quite sharply, particularly for those who are able to keep a job.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, I have decided that that should be increased.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, you are released but you are subject to supervision for five years, which, hopefully, will help in keeping you clean.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, the changes, taken as a whole, mean that if you have abusers who only consume drugs and admit to their drug use, they will undergo shorter but more intensive rehabilitation in the DRC as opposed to LT.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: And then, they will be placed on CBP, and then they will report for a longer period of supervision of up to five years.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: During the period of CBP and supervision, the abusers will be encouraged to hold a stable job, strengthen their relationship with their families and build better ties with the community.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, really, the aim is successful reintegration back into society and to reduce reoffending.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The journey is not an easy one for abusers.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: But we want to give them the best possible chance, and we want to motivate them to stay drug-free, and also put in the infrastructure like a longer period of supervision, which can help them in the long term.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clauses 13 and 14 give the Director of CNB the power to require abusers who have completed their rehabilitation, supervision or imprisonment to still report to CNB for urine or hair tests when required.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If the person fails to comply, then it is an offence, and the penalty could be an imprisonment or a fine, or both.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With the changes we implement, we obviously will track the recidivism rates very closely.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: If necessary, we will adjust our approach or change.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: A very substantial number, maybe up to one out of every two persons who are arrested, who would have gone to LT, could now go through this rehabilitation route that I have sketched out.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: As I mentioned earlier, those who could be charged would likely be persons who face other criminal charges or deny their drug use.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Sentencing trend for first-time drug consumption is usually six to eight months.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: With one-third remission, the period in custody will come down to four to five months.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Those charged and punished with imprisonment should serve a sentence that is more reflective of the strong deterrent stance against drugs.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They should not serve a period which is less than what a person in DRC would serve.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: The mandatory minimum sentence will also apply for first-time conviction for failure to provide a urine specimen or hair specimen.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: We have also reviewed the antecedents which count towards enhanced punishment for second-time abusers who are convicted in Court and LT.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: I will now briefly summarise the other amendments, which are really of a more operational or technical nature.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 5 repeals and re-enacts section 13 to clarify that the punishment for abetting an MDA offence in Singapore from outside of Singapore carries the same punishment as the primary offence abetted.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clauses 7 and 8 remove the powers of Vigilante Corps members for MDA offences, as they are no longer involved in drug operations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: They also extend the powers of "Special Police Officers" to conduct search and arrest for MDA offences, they are often involved in ground patrols or operations which may entail the arrest of drug offenders.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Special Police Officers will include full-time National Servicemen (NSFs) and operationally-ready (OR) National Servicemen during their periods of service.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clause 2 sets out the different categories of transport devices to make clear the different types, including unmanned craft, that enforcement officers may seize in the course of investigations.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clauses 6 and 8 define the related powers of search and seizure.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: Clauses 9 and 11 set out the processes and requirements for forfeiture, return and disposal.

speaker: The Minister for Home Affairs (Mr K Shanmugam)
text: So, we intend for these groups, like all other groups, to undergo post-release supervision to encourage them to stay drug-free.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: CNB officers, working with the wider Home Team, risk life and limb to deter the trafficking and consumption of drugs in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is only right that anti-drug laws are amended and updated to give the team of officers the needed powers and tools to deter and fight against pro-drug activity in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, significant amendments to the Misuse of Drugs Act being debated today are timely, useful and relevant.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Compared to many jurisdictions around the world, it can be said that Singapore does have the upper hand in the fight against drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But there is no reason why we should not continue making that upper hand more robust and stronger.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We can do this by training our focus and resources on the threats at hand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, 40% of total drug abusers were new drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Of those, about two-thirds were below the age of 30.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are the kinds of proportions we have been looking at year on year since 2015.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As the use of drugs leaves an indelible mark on the life of a person, the proportion of new drug abusers is particularly concerning.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: What is also of concern is the increasing number of youths who take on a drug-tolerant attitude towards drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This attitude towards drugs was more prevalent in older youth segments, that is, NSFs, university students and young working adults, than in younger youth groups, that is those from secondary school, junior college, polytechnic, Institutes of Technical Education (ITEs) and out-of-school youths.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One suggestion I have, in addition to the amendments proposed today, is that we include clear and informative learning material in our Ministry of Education (MOE) Science syllabus, which should detail the host of ills and harmful effects of experimenting with drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to start young and reinforce it regularly by putting it in the primary and secondary school syllabus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For university students, students travelling to places where drugs are more accessible, pre-exchange briefings, for example, could be arranged to remind them that drugs are not just illegal but also harmful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even as this offence provides tools to clamp down on contaminative actions and contain the spread of drug abuse, we cannot let this lull us into a sense of comfort.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We still need to continue to be vigilant in equipping people with the skills to (a) find credible sources of information and (b) guard against the rhetoric used by the pro-drug camp.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There are also other offences introduced by this Bill that seek to limit exposure and contaminative acts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: New section 11B introduces a new offence to protect our children against the harms of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, it requires a person who possesses drugs or drug paraphernalia not to leave them lying around where a child may unknowingly take it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In April 2017, in Utah, a girl was born – born a drug addict.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Her mother had used drugs heavily during her pregnancy.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But lest we think that this can only happen in Utah, here are some stories from newspapers that let us catch a small glimpse of how children are impacted by their parent’s drug abuse in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: One, in February 2018, a one-year-old boy was rescued from suspected drug traffickers after his caregiver left him in their care.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: When his mother was found later, she was four months pregnant and had tested positive for drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Two, in June 2018, a four-year-old girl was discovered with her mother – within reach of sachets of methamphetamine.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Three, in August 2018, a three-month-old girl was found in a unit with a suspected drug trafficker and drug abuser, with preliminary investigations showing that "ice" was abused during pregnancy and after the child was born.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: These are real-life stories of how drugs ruin lives, including that of innocent children.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, this new offence is important to protect children from harmful exposure to drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore must continue to take a firm and tough stance against drugs and questionable pro-drug narratives.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While these amendments to the MDA will put another tool in the legal toolbox for grappling with contamination and exposure to drugs, I would suggest that the medium of the Internet should be given special consideration.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because the Internet poses unique concerns.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Internet makes it easier to commit an offence and there is a greater potential for harm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is especially true when it comes to buying drugs online where the convenience and relative ease of accessing the Dark Net in the "comfort of one’s own home" makes it little more than a click away.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, to counterbalance these factors which make drug trafficking over the Internet easier, lucrative and also more harmful, we should have targeted offences or aggravated offences if the medium of the Internet is used.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Additionally, with the increase in online purchases, we need to make sure that our capacity to detect drugs in parcels will be able to match the volume being sent and received domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Another suggestion is that the MDA give due consideration to the potential harmfulness of the drug when mixed or cocktailed with available consumables.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We should not just be concerned about the weight of the illicit drug.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is because using such contaminants or mixers could make the cocktailed drug more addictive, more harmful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Related to this issue, there is a rapid proliferation in number, type and availability of new psychoactive substances worldwide.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to ensure that they are reclassified quickly into a First Schedule drug so that charges for trafficking, manufacture, import, export, possession or consumption can be made.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This will help reduce the demand for and supply of such drugs, that is, through deterrence.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides preventing the spread of drug abuse and a drug-tolerant culture, it is important to step up rehabilitation efforts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I support these key and important steps of promoting rehabilitation of drug addicts.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This Bill seeks to support rehabilitation efforts in a few ways and build on the ongoing excellent work of the Prisons Officers, counselling staff and voluntary welfare organisations (VWOs) and non-governmental organisations (NGOs) who put in tireless efforts in the area of rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is good in that it goes further to try to ensure that low-risk youths in the non-residential Youth Enhanced Supervision (YES) scheme are given the best shot at rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This amendment also recognises the importance of the family in rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Because the family can play an important role in providing not just practical support but also morale, encouragement and purpose in life, I hope that older drug abusers would also be given opportunities to engage their families, such as to help drug abusers reconcile with their families who could be their pillars of support upon release.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Would the Ministry consider the possibility of having more open visits, such as that reported by The Straits Times during the Children's Day in 2017, for suitable cases, especially for inmates with young children?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This increases the amount of time that our captains of lives have to work with drug addicts to rehabilitate and decrease recidivism.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This is excellent as there is greater support and accountability for a longer time during the integration phase.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With this longer supervision period, it is also important that supervision is not too disruptive so that the ex-offender's studies or employment will not be too affected.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With the possibility of hair tests, how often does an ex-offender need to report for testing?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For long-term resilience, could the Ministry consider providing some opportunities for physical activity or games so that former or recovering drug addicts can experience that there can be meaning to life and relief without drugs?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides increasing the time of the supervision order to decrease recidivism, would the Ministry consider giving a workbook for the ex-offenders to record and review what they have learnt in therapy sessions in relation to staying off drugs, for example, how they themselves can better cope with stress or how to replace drug cravings with sports?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This would provide them with a resource that they can have on hand whenever they may need to refer to it so as to assist in quashing the urge to take drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, because this Bill allows a supervision order to extend up to five years, it would be useful if the recidivism rate is tracked at the one-year, two-year, three-year, four-year and five-year marks.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Could the Minister please expand on the purpose behind this amendment and why seven days was chosen?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thirdly, there seems to be greater differentiation between drug abusers as a result of this Bill's amendments.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: At paragraph 19 of the Ministry of Home Affairs' (MHA's) press release relating to this Bill, it reads, and I quote, "However, drug abusers who commit other criminal offences and harm society will continue to be dealt with very strictly.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: They will be charged in Court and be liable for imprisonment and caning, including LT." Is this differentiation between those who commit other offences and those who do not, the reason why clause 16 introduces a tiered minimum punishment for consumption and possession offences?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Let us be clear that these amendments do not mean that Singapore's stance against drugs has softened.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We are still treating drug abuse as a clear menace which needs to be eradicated, not tolerated.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In fact, if we look at the Bill closely, the changes are actually mixed in strategy but single in purpose.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Clause 16 introduces minimum punishment for those charged and convicted for consumption or possession offences even though it is their first time.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, what is clear is that while some amendments are rehabilitation-focused, the law does not hesitate to be harsh when it needs to be.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: By consuming drugs, a drug user is harming himself or herself, his or her family, his or her community, and society.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even cannabis, which has been legalised in some countries, is harmful.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even though patients try to minimise the consequences of cannabis, treatment providers say that many report feeling isolated, paranoid and are unable to effectively interact with the outside world, and experience psychosis and hallucinations.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Colorado Springs, marijuana has even been called, and I quote, the "gateway drug to homicide" by a district attorney.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The impact is so great that there has been much local response to the harm marijuana is causing.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, why do we want a drug-free Singapore, not a drug reduced Singapore, not a drug tolerant Singapore, but a drug-free Singapore?

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: No insidious pro-drug camp should deter us from our view that drugs are, indeed, harmful – harmful to the abuser, their families, society and a country's human potential.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Indeed, Minister Shanmugam has taken this clear line on the international stage and I support it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I do not agree with questionable groups who push pro-drug rhetoric.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Singapore is on the right path in its tough stance against drugs.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must continually be on our guard, never taking a defeatist attitude.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have to look at threats beyond our shores in order to guard our shores.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There has also been international concern that the drug gangs there will diversify into other kinds of synthetic drugs, such as ketamine and fentanyl, which are highly addictive, highly destructive.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Rather, with legal amendments, such as these, the resolve is made even more steely.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As this Bill adds steel to Singapore's determination to deter a potential drug menace, I support it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Almost 20 years ago, the Ministry took a very specific approach towards hardcore addicts through the MDA, initiating long-term mandatory imprisonment and caning for hardcore drug addicts, a hardcore addict being warned, defined as having been caught more than twice for drug consumption.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Back then, the priority was not on framing drug addiction as a social issue afflicting drug addicts but a behaviour that has been criminalised.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In introducing the long-term regime, the then Minister moving the amendments noted that the proportion of hardcore addicts amongst the total drug rehabilitation centre population has increased from 65% in 1994 to 71% in 1997.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In his Second Reading speech, the Minister also referred to hardcore addicts as "bad people" who are likely to become drug pushers and traffickers, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The position revealed the state's philosophy that was focused on an uncompromising stance towards drug addicts, towards hardcore drug addicts, with rehabilitation openly seen as having its limits.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In the words of the then Minister, I quote, "Sometimes, despite all the good heartedness, the love and the hard work put in by volunteers in halfway houses, some of these volunteers do feel disheartened that these addicts just do not have the discipline to take the treatment.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Government will do what it can to help them, that is, both the recovering addicts as well as the halfway houses.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In terms of financial support, I think if we can justify a case to ask for more money, we will look at it.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Government does not just spend money, throwing good money after bad money to people who do not want to change."  One of the main amendments proposed today is to finetune the LT1 and LT2 regimes and circumstances where the drug addict does not have concurrent criminal charges.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Speaker, I am supportive of the aforesaid changes and commend the significantly more enlightened attitude taken by policymakers to shift the focus on helping selected repeat drug offenders in a more purposeful and surgical manner through the calibration of the MDA rehabilitation regime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is no mean feat, given the risks that some members of the public may erroneously construe this shift as a relaxation of attitude towards hardcore drug addiction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, I see it as an example of rational and sensible policymaking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In fact, this policy shift is significant, considering the LT regime was introduced a mere 20 years ago and to cover even more offenders when the Act was amended in 2006.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Notwithstanding my support on these points, I have some clarifications I want to seek from the Minister.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The first clarification is a request for information.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In 1998, the then Minister, in introducing the LT regime, shared that more than 73% of hardcore drug addicts have some form of a criminal record.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But the Minister also shared that, given easy access to funds and a general rise in access to drugs in the region, in view of these realities, and the latest statistics provided by the Minister in his Second Reading speech, would the Minister be able to share the family background and income levels of those with criminal charges and those without under the current LT1 and LT2 regimes?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, to give the public a better sense of the rehabilitation task ahead, can the Minister share, out of the inmates committed to DRCs, how many are repeat offenders to date?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The reality, when we speak of rehabilitation and the new calibrated approach, is that someone somewhere will be on the delivery end of the outcome sought – far fewer repeat drug addicts, compared to the current regime.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, the proposed changes are likely to put an acute focus on the people behind rehabilitation as they endeavour to get drug addicts out of a dangerous situation for good.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What sort of training and support will these individuals undergo so that they do not feel disheartened about addicts who do not respond well to treatment, such that they can continue plugging away at the hugely important task of rehabilitation?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This is likely to become more significantly as a large part of rehabilitation involves reintegrating the addicts into the community and in gainful employment, something that may be even more challenging in this age of economic destruction.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is vital that maximum support is extended to the volunteers, workers and supporters throughout the drug rehabilitation chain, from DRC staff to uniformed officers, CNB officers and to families and parents that need help and assistance to, in turn, help their loved ones and individuals under their care to kick the habit for good.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I will take the Chair at 4.20 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 4.01 pm until 4.20 pm.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A whole menu of drugs from cannabis, heroin, methamphetamine and others are commonly abused by teens and older persons, including women.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In light of this, it is, indeed, timely to review the Act and implement much needed revisions to address the issue.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Drug offenders nabbed by various CNB-led operations included Singaporeans and foreigners.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The number of new drug abusers also remained high.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But what is even more worrying, however, is the increasingly liberal attitudes towards drug abuse among young people.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: A news report in 2017 revealed that, in line with rising trends of drug abuse among young people, more of them expressed that they are willing to experiment with drugs for a new experience.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: This would not come as a surprise as more prolific use of social media means exposure to pop-media and a large population of youths in the West that normalises drug use.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: And, with more youngsters travelling, studying and working abroad where drugs are more accessible and even legal, certainly they would be able to find more opportunities to consume drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: In fact, I have seen young parents, both father and mother, go in and out of prison because of drug-related offences and that is why I brought up in this House recently, asking if there is any systematic ways of following up with those who have young children at home to make sure that their well-being is not compromised.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Criminalising such acts of contamination is a form of deterrence that could save the lives of many young people who could potentially become drug offenders.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, I am concerned about how this can be effectively enforced.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: We do not expect an offender to engage in a conversation, say, on how to use drugs, in an open setting.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The conversation is likely to be held in private and would only come to light if there is a whistleblower.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Perhaps, the only time this would come to light would be when the offence has been committed and the perpetrator squeals while under interrogation and there are records of text messages as evidence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Otherwise, I think it is difficult to enforce.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, in the case of young children who do not know what their parents are doing but then they are exposed to drugs because their parents are drug abusers, so, I just wonder, in cases like these, how is this law going to take action?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Having said that, criminalising this act could serve as a deterrent to get people to think twice before intentionally influencing others to be involved with drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The question that arises then is: what is the definition of instruction?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: What if someone asks a question about manufacturing drugs and another person gives answers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am sure the authorities do not mean to restrict genuine public education to create awareness as a deterrent against drug abuse.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we must also be aware that those who are curious about drugs can turn to the Internet where there is an abundance of materials to get information.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I am pleased to note that the existing rehabilitation programmes will be improved.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Drug addicts and offenders will certainly benefit from the increased counselling, supervision and longer detention.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: However, do we have sufficient resources and skilled counsellors to execute these programmes?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many prison counsellors do we currently have versus the population of drug abusers?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: How many more will we need to meet the requirements of the amendments?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: So, I wonder if we have the relevant support networks for our prison counsellors.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I know someone who does prison counselling work, and the nature of her job is such that she sometimes gets negatively affected, getting insomnia and even depressive feelings.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: I hope our prison counsellors and other professionals have a good care network as we have to ensure that their mental well-being is not being compromised in order for them to do their work well.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Additionally, what kind of benchmarks will be used to determine whether one is completely rehabilitated and ready to commit to a life that is completely drug-free and thus no longer requires supervision?

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: The Bill introduces some thoughtful new measures to enhance rehabilitation programmes and curb drug abuse through peer influence.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: But we have to get to the root of the problem.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is far more important to equip young people with the correct mindset and knowledge about drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: It is far more impactful if they make the decision to say no to drugs, rather than for authority figures to make the decision for them.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: (In Mandarin):   Surveys show that young Singaporeans are more and more liberal towards drugs, with 16% of them indicating that they are willing to try it out, while one-third of the respondents think that marijuana is harmless.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: As young people these days can easily access online information and more and more people are going overseas, they can easily be tempted by drugs.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, we should also pay attention to drug information that is originating from the Internet.

speaker: Er Dr Lee Bee Wah (Nee Soon)
text: Even without an introducer, someone who has his mind set on finding drug information will be able to find it on the net.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I salute our Government for maintaining strict control over the misuse of controlled drugs in Singapore, especially with the recent and timely amendments to the MDA to hold accountable any person knowingly or recklessly leaving controlled drugs exposed within a child's reach.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: We have seen many tragic stories of children ingesting such controlled drugs by accident which had resulted in overdose cases ending up in hospital emergency departments.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: At my recent attendance at the World Pharmacy Congress in Glasgow, I learned from pharmacists practising in Africa, Canada, the United Kingdom (UK) and the United States (US) about the worldwide issues regarding drug abuse.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The situation is currently out of control, resulting in countries no longer looking to curb the problem, but instead, resorting to setting up needle stations to try to, at the very least, prevent abusers from contracting the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) or Hepatitis C infections.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such a defensive approach does not attack the root cause of the problem.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The harm caused by the abuse of these substances on the abusers, their families and the society at large is devastating.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: First and foremost, even though the situation is much more controlled in Singapore due to our strict laws regarding drug trafficking, I still have my reservations and concerns for potential abuse in prescribing of controlled drugs in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Could this be just the tip of the iceberg?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: I quote Prof Tay Boon Keng, Emeritus Consultant and SMC Council member, who is also the Chairperson of the Ministry of Health (MOH) Opioid Guidance workgroup: "These past errant cases are all from the private health sector and tremendous expense was taken to take action (mostly legal) against these practitioners.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Such a move will allow pharmacists to provide oversight of such prescriptions, evaluate for appropriateness of use and duration of treatment, as well as contribute to national aggregated information to flag out high-risk prescribers or patients.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: The dispensing separation will add additional barriers to access for addicts and, hence, reduce opportunities for abuse, prevent unintended addiction to a significant extent by the general public, and safeguard physicians from such malpractices.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: With such ease of access to such substances overseas, how can we heighten public awareness, especially for our children going abroad to study during their formative years, so that they are more prepared for the potential risks?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can we incorporate such awareness programmes with "rehabilitated ex-offenders sharing their experiences" into briefing sessions for students before they go abroad?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Should we conduct more studies to find out the risk factors and reasons as to why these kids pick up such habits when they were away from home?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: To add on, cannabis may be the active ingredient in many non-medicinal products presented in a myriad of formulations, such as cigarettes, vaporisers, herbs, lotions and oils.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Some may mistakenly purchase these items innocuously, without knowing that the active ingredient is prohibited in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: How can we ensure that the public is well informed of these risks when they travel overseas and avoid unknowingly bringing in these illegal products when they return home?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Can we include a mandatory inflight education video/booklet for people departing and returning to Singapore?

speaker: Ms Irene Quay Siew Ching (Nominated Member)
text: Notwithstanding my proposal and concerns above, I stand to support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: (In Malay):  	I had relatives who were involved in drug addiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have personally seen how the drug problem can destroy someone's life and affect the family of the addict.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I understand and frequently hear about the challenges faced by addicts and their families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: We often discuss the drug problem in terms of statistics, policies or programmes.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: But the reality is very different for the addict and his family.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: As the Malay saying goes, as hard as it is to watch, it is even harder to the one shouldering the burden.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is certainly difficult when one makes a mistake and falls into drug addiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is extremely tough to kick the destructive habit, and the impact of the addiction can also affect the lives of families and the future of innocent children.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What usually happens is that when the addict leaves the rehabilitation centre, he finds it hard to return to normal life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Sometimes, these addicts have a hard time finding suitable jobs or they encounter challenges at the workplace due to stigma from society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: They will once again look for friends who will lead them back to drugs or they begin to get involved in other crimes to sustain their nasty habit.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It will be more complicated and more difficult to help the addict return to the right path.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I agree that all the current legislation in place has done much to help prevent the drug problem from becoming prevalent.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Tough laws are important in instilling fear to commit crime, described in English as having a deterrent effect.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, with a harsh and lengthy punishment, it will be more difficult for an addict to return to the workforce and reintegrate into society.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I hope that through experience, data and knowledge about rehabilitation, we can enhance the rehabilitation programmes in drug rehabilitation centres and continue giving support, if necessary, after the addict is released.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I think that this amendment, which carries a specific approach towards addicts with the objective of reforming them, is an encouraging one.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: It is hoped that this approach, as well as the joint efforts of our people, will help former addicts and their families continue to strengthen efforts to curtail the drug problem in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Singapore has always had a tough anti-drug stance and it is a position I fully support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I believe this Bill can further enhance the management of the misuse of drugs and addiction in Singapore.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate the refreshing approach towards the issue of drug addiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I have seen personally how challenging breaking the habit is for drug addicts and how severe addiction adversely impacts families.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I appreciate that some may see this as a softening in the approach towards addicts.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The fear is that addicts may not be deterred from abusing drugs because the penalty is not harsh enough and that these addicts can continue to be stuck in a loop and will remain social problems for the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: However, I believe that the targeted approach in building on the rehabilitation efforts could be a better long-term solution.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The effort in studying the rehabilitation process and building on our experience with drug rehabilitation centres can strengthen the rehabilitation regime and allow for more addicts to break the habit and have a new lease of life.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In addition, I am also not sure if we can say that imposing harsher penalties will yield better results.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: What we want to achieve is a drug-free society, a society that is resilient and improves over time.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Whether we like it or not, these addicts are part of our community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: The better option may be to work at the problem at its roots and break the addiction to the best of our ability, by providing the best recovery pathway and community support.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: I am, therefore, supportive of the proposed changes in this Bill that will allow for more focus on rehabilitation and reintegration of drug abusers into the community.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: In the course of my volunteer work in the past, I have come across anecdotes of children of addicts or those who live in the vicinity of drug abusers.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: These unfortunate young people are more likely to be influenced and entrapped into the unsavoury world of drug addiction.

speaker: Ms Rahayu Mahzam (Jurong)
text: Recently, I attended a focus group discussion on youths, and a volunteer shared that one of the children he was supervising at an after-school care centre told him that he was offered drugs by a group of men, presumably addicts, on his way back from school.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: (In Malay):   Sir, the Misuse of Drugs (Amendment) Bill that is tabled intends to further enhance preventive, eradication and rehabilitative measures so that the current efforts to manage the drug menace will be more effective overall.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: First, I would like to refer to sections 11B (1) and (2) that are being introduced via clause 3.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Sections 11B (1) and (2) were introduced because CNB had faced situations during their operations whereby addicts left the drugs or paraphernalia used to take drugs which were exposed to children.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The exposure of children to such situations may eventually cause these children to also take drugs.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The irresponsible behaviour of the adults mentioned earlier is truly deplorable.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As an adult, especially as a father or head of family, it is their responsibility to inculcate positive values in a child.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Unfortunately, such individuals not only neglect their responsibility, but, in fact, the actions mentioned earlier will or can cause damage in the young life of the child, as described in a Malay proverb which means "the one responsible for giving protection instead destroys what it is supposed to protect." Therefore, the introduction of sections 11B (1) and (2) is timely and appropriate.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have heard from several individuals, who are daily-rated employees, that they had to forgo their income for the day because they had to report for the test.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For these individuals, forgoing the daily income results in a huge loss and it also impacts their family’s daily expenses.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: These individuals usually have a less stable psychosocial condition.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: They need a more supportive environment that gives them an opportunity in their efforts to make a fresh start in life by becoming a responsible breadwinner.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: However, Sir, for these individuals, they will see a situation where they lost their daily income because they have to report for the tests as an obstacle and it will result in them feeling that the authorities are hindering them from performing their responsibility to take care of their families.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Although this matter may be seen as a minor issue by some, it is not a minor issue at all to the affected individuals.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I welcome this amendment because I believe that this new approach will result in more specific and effective efforts for each group.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also welcome the increasing use of psychology and psychotherapy approaches in the current rehabilitative programmes.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: The use of appropriate and specific approaches for these two groups will result in a more satisfying outcome.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For example, the approach taken for first-time offenders with low and medium risk should give emphasis on being remorseful about the offence committed and, at the same time, plant the seeds of hope in the offender whereby they can still work towards a better future.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I agree with this approach because an individual’s transformation process requires the involvement of immediate family members so that they understand their role in facilitating the offender’s transformation process.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the same reason, I hope that this requirement will also include the husband or wife of a young offender who is married, or individuals who have a family with their partners.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I also request for some flexibility whereby a suitable time to attend counselling sessions can be given to offenders and their family members so that it does not impact their efforts to earn an income.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Each and every one of us can play a part and contribute towards this effort.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: For the Malay community, we are grateful to have individuals and organisations who are committed and are actively involved in efforts to tackle the drug problem, for example, the late Mr Harun Ghani, a highly respected individual in the Malay community.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: I have personally heard from ex-addicts who paid tribute to the sincere efforts and selflessness of the late Mr Harun Ghani in helping them and their families throughout his life.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: Even though he is no longer with us, his efforts are still continuing in the form of the Harun Ghani Education Fund (HGEF), which is a fund to help the children of drug addicts, ex-addicts and also counsellors who are actively involved in helping offenders.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: This is described in a Malay proverb, which means, "the good deeds of a man will never be forgotten." The Hira Society is a VWO established and managed by Ustaz Razman bin Saridin.

speaker: Mr Muhamad Faisal Bin Abdul Manap (Aljunied)
text: As previously shared by Ustaz Razman himself, he was previously involved in drugs but has turned his life around and he embarked on this noble effort to help those caught in the world of drugs to rebuild their lives.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Deputy Speaker, Sir, Singapore has been described by many as having the toughest laws against the misuse of drugs in the world.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: And we continue to be unrelenting in our fight against drugs in a global environment which seems to be going in the opposite direction, becoming more liberal towards drugs, with more countries considering or already implementing drug decriminalisation.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singaporeans are travel addicts and have access to information and news from all over the world.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is inevitable that we compare our nation with other regimes, particularly the west.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In fact, for many of us who fly into Singapore, we are often given the announcement, in no certain terms, that Singapore has very harsh penalties against drug offences.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So, in this respect, some of us may ask, are our drug laws too antiquated, too draconian?

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a doctor, I cannot emphasise enough the damage illicit drugs can wreak upon one's body, much of which is irreversible.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: But you do not need a doctor to tell you this.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is the Government's duty to protect its people from harm and, hence, its firm stance on drugs should be supported and applauded.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Our traditional position had been to set firm and harsh penalties for those involved in drugs, to serve as a deterrent.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: So far, our measures had been quite effective for an open economy which welcomes visitors and the free flow of goods and services.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Ministry is now attempting a more calibrated approach to segment drug abusers who only take drugs from those with other concurrent criminal offences.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Currently, drug abusers arrested for the first and second time undergo rehabilitation at the DRC.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The plan is, of course, to better help all drug abusers break this vicious cycle of addiction and reintegrate into society sooner.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While I fully support the decision to focus more on rehabilitation and move away from penalties for first-time offenders, I am concerned that this approach may be perceived to be soft – a slap on the wrist – and may send the wrong signal to those tempted to experiment with drugs.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In the past, most drug addicts were dropouts from school or from troubled or lower-income families.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We also have anecdotal feedback from CNB and lawyers who observe more youths of both genders, across wider income and education spectrums, testing positive for drugs after returning from overseas trips or studies.

speaker: Dr Chia Shi-Lu (Tanjong Pagar)
text: If they perceive that they would be treated more leniently because they are first-time offenders, would not they perhaps be more open to trying out drugs?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
