text: I will speak on the welfare of the family, which is a key goal of our drug policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Before I discuss my specific concerns, I wish to commend the Government for devoting a significant part of this Bill and policy to focusing on the rehabilitation of the drug abuser.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Protecting our youths against exposure to drug abuse must be a central plank of our drug abuse policy.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must take a stern view of family members who abuse their position of trust by encouraging drug abuse in the youth.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: My concern is that section 11B(1) sets an extremely low bar for criminalising reckless exposure of drugs to youths.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The examples given in the Explanatory Notes to the Bill confirm that 11B(1) is aimed at deterring drug abusers from casually or recklessly exposing youths to drugs in a family setting even when there is no intent to encourage the youths to consume the said drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: First, there is the question of risks versus benefits to the family unit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I agree that all measures should be taken to prevent exposure of the youths to drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: At the same time, the drug abuser subject to section 11B(1) is a family member who may be a parent or a breadwinner.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Having that family member at home, provided they are not actively abusing drugs, is likely to be beneficial to the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The problem is similar to that of child abuse and neglect, where we must decide whether the child is better served by removal from the family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In fact, research by economist Joseph Doyle, published in the American Economic Review in 2007, shows that at-risk children have better long-term outcomes when they remain at home instead of being fostered.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Of course, if the drug abuser is encouraging drug consumption within the family, section 11B and all measures should be employed to separate the drug abuser from their family.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: But otherwise, the aim must remain the rehabilitation of the drug abuser to restore the functioning of the family unit as soon as possible.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Second, there is the issue of disparate impact.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Drug abuse is a problem that cuts across all strata of society.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: However, drug abuse is particularly hard on the less well-off who have fewer resources to cope in general.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Our less well-off drug abusers may live in family settings not because they want to expose their family to drugs, but because they cannot afford separate living quarters.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike some criminal justice systems, Singapore has been careful to avoid drug policies that criminalise to a disparate extent drugs associated with underprivileged socio-economic classes or minorities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: This is important because it ensures that our drug policies have broad support, and they are not seen as a policy that targets specific communities.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: We must do everything we can to ensure that our drug policy targets all abusers, regardless of class or status.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Third, we have existing laws that may already apply to the problem of youth exposure to drugs, and I would like to understand the Minister's views on why these may be insufficient.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Part II of the Children and Young Persons Act (CYPA) already criminalises acts that contribute to the delinquency or endangerment of children.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, the proposed section 11B(2) criminalises permitting or failing to take reasonable steps to prevent a young person from consuming controlled drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: So, is this an issue of the penalties under CYPA not being sufficient, or the threshold for prosecution under the proposed section 11B(2) being too high?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, as a matter of policy, would offenders in section 11B(1) also be subject to prosecution under CYPA?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Next, section 11B must also deter reckless exposure to be effective.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike the question of drug trafficking, where the offence is premeditated, the offence of reckless exposure may, by definition, result from thoughtless negligence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: A drug abuser may have no intention of encouraging their children to consume drugs, and yet, they may fail to take necessary care when securing their own drugs.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The question is whether the Ministry's experience in the field is that 11B(1) is likely to motivate drug offenders to take strong precautions to limit harm to their family members.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: While I understand estimating a counter-factual outcome is difficult, I would like to hear the Minister’s views on the deterrent effect of 11B(1).

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Such a report would evaluate the extent of recklessness involved, and the ability of the drug abuser to contribute meaningfully to the family unit.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Combating drug abuse must be a whole-of-Government problem.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In Tamil):   May I wish Happy Pongal to all those who celebrate the Pongal festival.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: May your homes and hearts be filled with joy forever.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: (In English): I support this Bill as it enhances and strengthens the MDA to effectively and comprehensively tackle the issue of drug abuse in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Today, I wish to speak on two areas of concern: prevention and integration.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: These statistics seem to underline a growing trend among the young in taking a more liberal attitude towards drug abuse, influenced by pro drug-related content.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This was one of the conclusions drawn by the Youth and Public Perception Survey by the National Council Against Drug Abuse (NCADA).

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Online peddling of drugs has also been flagged out as a rising concern by CNB.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: What efforts are undertaken by the authorities to counter these influences and online drug peddling?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Are there plans to flag out and perhaps block such contents or access to websites promoting the use of harmful drugs?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Unlike the past, more of today’s drug abusers hail from middle and even upper middle-class families, with parents having no history of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Undergraduates, NSFs and young working adults are taking drugs, with some even going overseas to consume drugs thinking they can evade detection and prosecution.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Can I propose that the authorities introduce a mandatory anti-drug course as part of NS?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Having just completed my reservist, I believe NSmen can also benefit from this training.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In tertiary educational institutions, can I suggest we have organisations, such as NCADA, step up engagements with students by tying up with student bodies and training these youths to be Anti-drug Ambassadors on campus?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: There are currently many efforts aimed at addressing this growing pro-drug trend, including the recent media campaign launched by NCADA and the ongoing Dadah Itu Haram campaign, as well as the annual activities and efforts by CNB.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: But based on my interactions with youths from all spectrums, I have found that these campaigns are quite effective at reminding the mainstream youths, but not as effective at targeting the youths who are more at risk of drug abuse due to gang influence or other delinquency issues.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: One step towards targeting those youths-at-risk is this Bill's efforts to criminalise acts by adults who expose children to the risks of drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Often, these adults are the children’s own parents.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Parents who do not seem to care that if you expose a child, who does not know better, to drugs, you condemn him to a life of misery and addiction.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: We must protect our vulnerable young from reckless parents or adults.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: In the same light, I would also like to support this Bill's move to grant the Director of CNB the power to require possibly negligent parents or guardians to attend counselling to rehabilitate low-risk youth abusers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: As they say, it takes a village to raise a child.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I say we must do our part to fight and stamp out drug abuse, starting with the young.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I also understand that Singapore is studying successful models of engagement from Iceland and Finland to tackle the drug issue effectively.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Can the hon Minister share if Singapore will be adapting or implementing these models or have drawn lessons from them to improve our local efforts?

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: He also shared of plans to have counselling sessions via video-conferencing and an App containing self-help resources and a database for jobs for former offenders.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: This is a welcome move to better rehabilitate former offenders and it shows the commitment of our officers.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Drug offenders who have been released from prison or DRC face a lot of obstacles in their efforts to reintegrate themselves into society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: They navigate a world with a stigma on their backs, while coping with their obligations to report for mandatory urine tests at designated police divisions while trying to avoid some of their peers who may draw them back into drugs.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Many of these supervisees work simple jobs as delivery or dispatch riders on a part-time basis.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Due to inflexible reporting timings or delays in taking their urine test, their jobs are affected and, in some extreme cases, they are laid off.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Some of these supervisees are even putting off finding a job just because the potential employers cannot accommodate them taking time off for urine tests.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Such gathering points while waiting to take urine tests provides a platform for ex-offenders who may be still active in illicit drug activities to prey on fellow ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I hope that MHA could look into this issue to make the process less painful for those who are sincerely and genuinely trying to turn over a new leaf and find a stable employment.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: Through such programmes, I hope more former drug offenders will come forward to help and perhaps mentor and even serve as a role model to those struggling with drug addiction to overcome and reintegrate back into the society.

speaker: Mr Mohamed Irshad (Nominated Member)
text: I think we have a good regime in Singapore that balances deterrence and strict enforcement against drugs while providing as many opportunities as possible to drug offenders to turn around their lives.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Every country is affected by the scourge of drugs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In some countries, it has, in fact, worsened.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We can expect ourselves to be repeatedly targeted by syndicates as a transit point as well as a market for illicit drugs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The need to protect Singapore from drugs is even more critical now.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And second, that a more finely calibrated rehabilitation approach will be useful in addressing our drug situation in the longer run.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: This is a careful balance to manage but critical if we are to continually improve our drug situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, we must ensure that we continue our zero-tolerance approach to drugs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: We have adopted a comprehensive and consistent approach to tackling both drug supply and demand.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In 2015, the number of drug abusers arrested comprised less than 0.1% of our population.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Would-be and current drug offenders know that the consequences are dire, whether the offences are committed in Singapore or overseas.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, a no-compromise approach to drugs does not mean that we cannot and should not evolve towards better means of improving the overall drug situation.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: First, what are these offences of harm to society?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: And second, if an offender commits drug and unrelated criminal offences sequentially but within a short timeframe, would he still be eligible for EDSO?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The move towards greater focus on rehabilitation recognises that we must focus on helping the offender to kick the habit as a longer-term outcome.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Yet, we must calibrate this against the potential harm to society as well.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: There are two important points in the anti-drugs policy.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: One, to prevent would-be offenders from getting started on drugs.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Under the non-custodial EDSO regime, how can we position this publicly so that it is not seen as a light-touch approach for young people wanting to experiment with drugs?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: For the drug offenders, the term "LT" or "Long Term Imprisonment" is much feared.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The punishment of long minimum imprisonment sentences and mandatory caning can deter addicts from continuing their habits.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: I have often heard from offenders at my Meet-the-People Sessions (MPS) or even when I was a Police Officer that they will tell me "No more drugs already, next time it is LT." It also protects society from potential harm from sustained demand for drugs feeding a drug market.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: By removing the threat of LT from these drug offenders, would this send a conflicting signal from our zero-tolerance policy?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In addition, is the time limit of one year in DRC for first-time abusers too short or can we consider longer sentences for subsequent offences?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Furthermore, we know that offenders in jail must follow rules and adhere to a rigid regime.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: It has been suggested in some research that, for drug addicts, their isolation from society for a period of time, where they go cold turkey, might make recovery easier.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Those who enter the DRC track have a whole host of other challenges to manage.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: They must find a job, go for urine tests, and learn how to say "no" to friends who ask them to do drugs again.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: So, are we prepared to also explore a policy whereby both imprisonment sentences and DRC work hand-in-hand in order to achieve a better longer-term outcome?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: People who are tempted to try and who become addicted to drugs, are robbed of the opportunity to live life to the fullest.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Let us ensure that our top priority is still a zero-tolerance anti-drug policy.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It is a very timely one, particularly with the new year festivities just over a couple of weeks ago where several police arrests over drug abuse and dealings had been made in several countries.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: For instance, at the recent end-of-year Field Day Festival in Sydney, Australia, there were more than 150 arrests made of young people abusing drugs at the festival, with six arrests due to drug supply and trafficking.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Over the new year weekend in Louisville, Kentucky, in the US, a group of 40 people were arrested for drug abuse.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Out of the 40 people, 14 were below 18 years old.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In Belfast, Ireland, five deaths were recorded involving young people in their late teens to late 20s due to a prescription drug overdose during the Christmas period.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Belfast Mater Hospital claimed that there has been a spike in the number of cases of prescription drug overdose in young people, some as young as 13.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These prescription drugs, such as Xanax and Lyrica, are sold illegally on the streets.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: These incidents are a serious cause for concern.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It does not help that illicit drugs are now also available through the dark web, as well as in some jurisdictions that have relaxed their legislation against personal or recreational drug use.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In addition to the relatively easier availability of drugs on the streets or through online means, access to drugs in the home exacerbates the problem of drug abuse by minors and children.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I quote Dr Mike Males, who is a senior researcher for the Center on Juvenile and Criminal Justice in the US and a former professor at the University of California Santa Cruz: "California’s and America's drug fatality crisis is firmly centred in whites and middle-agers.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: California's 5.7 million white men aged 25 and older account for 40% of drug deaths.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: That is more than the total drug deaths among the state's 24 million Latino, African and Asian Americans of both sexes and all ages.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: True, many adult drug problems began in teen or young adult years.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: However, adult drug and family abuses are major factors in teens abusing drugs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The problem is circular and must be addressed with integrated strategies across families and communities." The role of significant adults – parents, guardians and teachers – in a child's life cannot be underestimated and will have substantial impact on how that child turns out.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This is also true when it comes to developing lifelong and life-changing habits.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The struggle with marijuana abuse by Nick Sheff has been shared widely by his father, American journalist David Sheff.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: In his first revelation about his son's struggle with marijuana abuse that was published in the New York (NY) Times Magazine, David shared that "Indeed, when he was 12, I discovered a vial of marijuana in his backpack.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I met with his teacher, who said: ''It's normal.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Most kids try it.'' Nick said that it was a mistake – he had been influenced by a couple of thuggish boys at his new school – and he promised that he would not use it again.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: You can read David's article published in the NYTimes Magazine dated 6 February 2005, titled "My Addicted Son" or you can watch the movie "Beautiful Boy" to feel the pain and anguish both David and Nick went through in trying to overcome Nick's marijuana addiction.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: It may be easy to point fingers at his then 6th grade teacher, or even at David himself, who smoked recreational marijuana with his son Nick.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Our home must remain a warm and loving sanctuary for our children, and not a worm hole to hell.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under clause 3, particularly sections 11B and 11C, will enforcement actions be taken only on the drug abuser or will other adult family members who are non-drug users within the household also be convicted if drugs are found within the reach of a child or minor within the home?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Under clause 19, section 34A, how many counselling sessions will the parents be involved in?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why do we not make it compulsory for the counselling sessions to involve both the parents and the young drug user or supervisee?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Why leave it as "whether or not together with the supervisee"?

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To me, having both the parents and the young drug user go through the entire counselling process and rehabilitation journey together will be useful in addressing the causes of drug use in the first place, and not merely addressing the symptoms.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I recall meeting a couple who are parents at my Meet-the-People Session more than a year ago, who shared about their son's foray into drug use while serving NS.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: At this point, Mr Deputy Speaker, please allow me to speak in Malay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In Malay):   Drug abuse is an issue that continues to haunt us.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Although drug offences carry harsh punishments, where the offenders can be jailed for life or given the death penalty if found guilty of drug trafficking, the number of drug abusers and drug traffickers in our community is still high, more than what we want it to be.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: I have met my constituents at the MPS who shared stories about their husbands or wives being nabbed by CNB for taking drugs in their own homes.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: As adults, we cannot neglect our responsibilities towards our children in shaping their habits or lifestyle, especially in instilling them with positive behaviour and helping them stay away from bad habits or addictions like drug abuse.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We are the pillars of the family, and as the Malay saying goes, the sap from the leaf will trickle down its stalk, that is, children will imitate what their parents do.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: (In English): In conclusion, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, the perils of drug abuse are very real, and no sufficient amount of legislative changes can fully protect our loved ones from the dangers of drugs.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: We still need preventive education, awareness and an abundance of love and care and continued vigilance to keep drugs at bay.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Nonetheless, these legislative changes we are debating today are needed to ensure there is protection for our loved ones and that the necessary enforcement action can be taken to ensure that very protection for them.

speaker: Dr Intan Azura Mokhtar (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Notwithstanding the questions and clarifications I have, I support the amendments to the MDA.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Singapore has always taken a hard stance on drugs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Hon Members who spoke before me support this stance.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a reflection of our understanding of the pernicious effects that drugs and drug addiction have on our communities, and the need to ensure that drug consumption does not become an entrenched habit in our society.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a recognition in recent years that whilst it remains necessary to ensure that our laws deter drug trafficking, possession and consumption, there is also a need for a broader range of measures to rehabilitate offenders to mitigate the risk of relapse.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The proposed amendments to the Act serves these two purposes – enhancing our enforcement powers against drug-related activities, especially where young children are concerned and, at the same time, strengthening the drug rehabilitation regime by taking a more calibrated approach vis-a-vis drug abusers.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Taking into account remission, the length of imprisonment is approximately between four and five months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: At the same time, the present regime also contemplates rehabilitation in the DRC for first-time offenders with no criminal record, and this is generally a term of approximately eight months.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand that the proposed amendments would address the existing disparity, namely, that a first-time offender who is unsuitable for DRC, for example, if he had committed other offences, together with a drug consumption offence, and is sentenced to imprisonment, he would serve a shorter term than a first-time offender who is deemed suitable and sentenced to undergo treatment at a DRC.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: If the focus is to address this disparity, why not put this before the Court, rather than impose a mandatory minimum sentence?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The Court will then have a discretion to impose a sentence that suits the circumstances of the case, for example, drawing a distinction in sentencing between the consumption of a Class A drug, which is more serious, versus a Class C drug.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: After all, the sentence should take into account the circumstances of each individual offender, to distinguish between their differing degrees of criminal culpability.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The existing provisions allow the Courts this flexibility.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is encapsulated by a High Court decision, where the Court said, "Adopting this wider spectrum of sentencing options for first-time offenders will allow adequate regard to be duly given to the many imponderables involved when such offences are committed, such as: what was the amount of drug(s) consumed… what was the occasion that led to the act of consumption; was it planned or incidental to some other event… was any payment involved; is the accused a first-time drug consumer, a casual consumer or an addict?

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: While this is by no means a comprehensive or exhaustive list, it is intended to highlight some of the thought processes a sentencing judge should apply when determining the appropriate custodial sentence for drug consumption offences.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given that not all offences of consumption are the same, it follows that not all acts of consumption ought to be punished identically with a rigid, immutable starting point that constitutes an end by itself." This is not to say that the Courts would treat drug possession or drug consumption lightly.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In the same case, the Court expressly recognised that a fine may be imposed in very limited instances where a young offender with no antecedents is involved, and even then, this cannot be an invariable practice for all young offenders.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Additionally, there need not be parity between the DRC regime and imprisonment, in terms of the length of time, given that they serve different purposes.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We are not necessarily comparing apples with apples.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: A DRC incarceration is not a conviction, and the primary purpose of DRC is to rehabilitate, which understandably requires some time.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, a person dealt with by the Courts, convicted and sentenced will have a conviction record.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: And the aims of imprisonment also include retribution and deterrence, rather than a pure focus on rehabilitation.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: My concern is that there could be situations where it does not make sense for a person to be sentenced to a DRC, and yet it may not make sense for the person to be sentenced to a one-year imprisonment term, for example, a foreign national who commits a drug offence while on a social visit pass.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is little utility in sending him to a DRC for rehabilitation, given that he is not resident in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But with the amendments, the Court will now have no choice but to sentence him to imprisonment for at least one year, even if the offence may be on the relatively less culpable side.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I understand from the hon Minister's speech that this is because the focus is on making sure that the drug addict is fully rehabilitated and the chances of recidivism is reduced.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: As I understand it, if a drug addict beyond the five-year mark does not take drugs, then, the chances are, he would not take drugs in the future.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Before I end, Mr Deputy Speaker, Sir, I would like to pay tribute to the good work of the CNB officers over the years since CNB was established in 1971.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We had a serious problem with drugs then.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: This is a stark memory for me because, as a young boy, I grew up in a neighbourhood where I played football almost every day with some very talented footballers who could perform mesmerising tricks.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: They could have made it into the national squad.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: But they could not make it into the national squad because they became addicted to drugs and their whole lives were wasted.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: It was the Government and CNB's tough and uncompromising stance against drugs that allowed us to emerge from that dark situation to now enjoy a relatively drug-free and low-crime environment.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I highlight low crime because there has always been a link between drug-taking and crime.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Many drug addicts resort to crime to be able to fund their habit.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: There is also a positive economic impact arising from the successful tackling of the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: We managed to ensure that the people who would otherwise be snagged by the lure of drugs, would be economically active and contribute to their families and our country.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: In contrast, a good number of countries have gone the opposite way.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: She also found that opioid addiction has led to less economic participation amongst her people.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: I highlight this not to gloat but really to join in the suggestion that the hon Member Mr Christopher de Souza made, in terms of highlighting these cases to people who may otherwise take a softer stance to drugs.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: Given our geographical proximity to the centres of production of controlled drugs, higher levels of drug production, as the hon Minister said, as well as our status as an international transport hub, we could easily be in the same situation as in the US, if not for our dedicated and courageous officers working in tandem with other Government agencies, and critically, with the whole-hearted support of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Murali Pillai (Bukit Batok)
text: The job that our CNB officers do on a day-to-day basis is clearly not for the faint-hearted, as the people that they deal with, especially the drug traffickers, tend to be more desperate and violent, given the stakes should they get apprehended.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It is important to review the existing framework to ensure that we are up to date with the evolving drug landscape.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Just last week, at a visit to the new Selarang Halfway House, Minister Shanmugam announced a three-pronged approach to better rehabilitate ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This includes assigning inmates to the same case officer for the entire period of incarceration, focusing more on correctional programmes targeted at individuals, and getting more family and community support.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In light of the refocus on rehabilitation, can the Minister clarify the rationale behind introducing mandatory minimum sentences and enhanced penalties and how this might be consistent with the broader strategy for addressing repeat commission of drug offences?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Both legislative and executive action should be aligned to present a coherent message on our renewed commitment to rehabilitation and reintegration.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The family is an important part of the rehabilitative process.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is already a clear sign that inmates lack family support and this problem might have existed prior to the drug problem.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Strained family ties were perhaps one of the reasons they consumed drugs in the first place.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In the same vein of embracing a more whole-family approach, I hope we will also consider a greater push towards a more forgiving and rehabilitative approach to all drug offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond focusing on young offenders, we should also help inmates currently serving their sentences to maintain social connections with their immediate family.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The family serves as an important social safety net upon the inmates' release.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Families help to support inmates' efforts to change, reintegrate into society as responsible citizens and reduce the reoffending rates.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Research has shown that family support is a key factor that prevents inmates from reoffending.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I have suggested this before, and I hope that we can consider removing the glass panel between inmates and their children more often.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Today, family bonding and interaction with inmates' children are too limited.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Family support, especially interaction with their children, could strengthen the resolve of inmates to change their lives for the better.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Stopping parental contact with their child could cause resentment, a sense of abandonment on both sides and weaken the social support structure for an inmate.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This works against our objective of a supportive rehabilitation process and also negatively affects the child.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There is precedence to remove the separation by glass panel on special occasions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: On Children's Day in 2017, some inmates at the Tanah Merah Prison were allowed an open visit where they could hug and hold their loved ones.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some of the inmates had not seen their children for four years until that visit.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Having physical contact with their families can be a strong reminder for inmates to turn over a new leaf for their families.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As stated by the spokesperson for Focus on Family Singapore, "Humans thrive when we know we are loved.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: When inmates connect and are reconciled with their families, there is a lower chance of them reoffending." I would also like to take this opportunity to applaud MHA for increasing support for ex-offenders.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Development and Reintegration Programme is promising and aims to help inmates upon their release.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: It provides continuity of care from prisons to the community, to help the inmates better reintegrate and prevent reoffending.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the support offered after ex-offenders are released, I also hope we can provide more support to inmates while they are in prison, especially during the initial incarceration phase and especially by ex-offenders who have managed to turn their lives around.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I had raised this before during the Committee of Supply debates and I hope the Ministry could consider including more programmes featuring ex-offenders and imparting life-changing strategies at this initial stage, especially during the initial two to three months, when inmates are most motivated to change and commitments are more sustainable.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Drug addiction turns healthy people with potential into zombies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Drug dealers are not interested in killing their sources of income.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Their best customers are addicts who manage to stay alive, keep buying for a while and help recruit new customers.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: One of my greatest worries is how we deal with the ease of accessing drug suppliers through the Internet, social networking and messaging platforms, such as WhatsApp, which provides end-to-end encryption.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Another issue I am deeply concerned about is how drugs still manage to find their way into Singapore despite our strict laws.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How thorough are our checks on items being transported in?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I conclude with my support for the Bill.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This is evident through the introduction of the new sections 11B, 11C and 11D.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am in general support of these amendments to the MDA.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We are beginning to see a more nuanced and calibrated approach to drug rehabilitation by MHA.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: There is a continued focus in helping drug abusers break the cycle of addiction more effectively and reintegrate into society sooner.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend this intent, especially given that we all agree neither criminalisation nor imprisonment is viewed as the miracle solution.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: However, our drug rehabilitation regime still tacitly acknowledges the stigma associated with drug use and addiction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Even without the World Health Organization declaring that addiction to illicit drugs is the most stigmatised, it is not hard to surmise that social isolation and marginalisation hamper the effectiveness of even the most effective rehabilitative efforts.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Public education and policy realignment in the direction of destigmatising drug addiction can and should complement institutionalised drug rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: At the moment, it would not be a misstatement to say that illicit drug use and addiction are met with great social disapproval.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Commonly held perceptions of persons with drug addictions are that they are weak in resolve, irresponsible and out to have a good time at society's expense.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In short, addiction is viewed as a moral failing, and the associated harms of addiction considered wholly self-inflicted.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I believe that it is time we challenge the common wisdom that shame, a fundamental element of stigmatisation, is the best way to respond to undesired social behaviours and habits, especially in light of advances in neurobiology research which validate the characterisation of addiction as a brain disease tied to changes in brain structure and function.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Advances in the field of neurobiology show that addiction causes deficits to the functioning of the prefrontal cortex.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: While I have been informed that these studies have not been researched in our local context, some have been co-published by researchers hailing from, amongst others, our very own Department of Pharmacology at the Yong Loo Lin School of Medicine, Yale University, Imperial College London and the National Institute on Drug Abuse in the US.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: In lay terms, addiction impairs the brain in ways which weaken the brain regions involved in executive functions, such as decision-making, inhibitory control and self-regulation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: It is easy to surmise, given this impairment, that stigma or externally-imposed shame would only provide very minimal, if at all, effective support or incentive for individuals who are seeking to quit their drug addictions.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Additionally, according to a study published by the US National Institute on Drug Abuse, stigma towards addiction also externalises in practical ways, for example, lower priority in healthcare policies, such as insurance.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Conversely, I believe that if we are able to align (a) the public’s understanding of drug use, (b) our public health policies on drug misuse, as well as (c) our institutionalised drug rehabilitation programmes with the brain disease model of addiction, we could start creating the right conditions for decreasing or, who knows, even preventing, drug misuse and addiction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Similar recommendations have been made in studies published by researchers on drug abuse.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: For clarity, Mr Deputy Speaker, I am not saying that Singapore must soften its stance on the statutory prohibition of drugs.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Rather, I am very encouraged by the widespread success of our whole-of-Government effort on War on Diabetes.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: That effort addresses the misconceptions and stigma, and has also begun to make headway in structural changes within business and community to influence social behaviours and habits.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: This would also support our public education programmes as shared earlier.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: First, the offences set out in section 11B apply to persons of or above 21 years of age in relation to exposing or permitting a child to drug use.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: The section also defines "child" to mean any person below 16 years of age.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: If this omission was unintentional, may I then ask the Minister what effects this drafting might nonetheless give rise to?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Second, clause 16 both (a) introduces minimum sentences for some offences where there was previously none, and (b) enhances punishment of an offender convicted of certain offences.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, clause 17 introduces enhanced penalties for a person who is convicted of certain offences under the Act and has certain antecedents.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Aside from a clear and continued emphasis on the severity of drug-related offences, I wish to ask the Minister what specific goals these amendments are intended to achieve and how they do so.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, I wish to ask the Minister if and how these amendments strike an appropriate balance between criminal penalty and rehabilitation.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Further, in what ways does this provision ensure that the psychosocial support programmes, if any, put in place with a view to include parents and guardians are able to serve their intended purpose?

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Studies have found that illicit drug users and persons with drug addiction are unable, due to social stigma, shame and guilt, to connect in healthy ways with fellow human beings thereby impeding their recovery and social integration.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Perhaps this is why it has been said that the opposite of addiction is not sobriety, it is human connection.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I commend the Ministry for taking the first steps in the right direction with a more human-centred approach with these new amendments.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, beyond taking the legal, medical and institutionalised approach, we must have a concerted community response to this adaptive challenge of drug misuse and addiction.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: Social integration without destigmatisation is a job half done!

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: We must remain open to evolving strategies as well as new social and scientific research that continue to put the human in the centre of our laws and their implementation on drug misuse and rehabilitation efforts.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: As a former Police Officer, I have seen how the problems associated with drug abuse extends beyond just the individual.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It affects family, friends and, ultimately, harms society.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore needs to continue with our firm stand of zero-tolerance towards drug abuse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is, therefore, timely and crucial that we review the MDA and make necessary amendments to safeguard public interest and prevent the rise in first-time abusers.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, I do have some questions and suggestions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, I agree with the measures introduced to make it an offence to expose children to drugs and permit young persons to consume drugs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Exposing the young to drugs causes addiction to become intergenerational and we must strive to eradicate such cases in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, the young are not just the only ones susceptible to the temptation of drugs, if drugs are left easily within reach.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There seems to be an increasing trend among the public displaying more liberal attitudes towards drugs, as evidenced through the 2015/2016 survey conducted by the National Council Against Drug Abuse.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an alarming trend and those who have not seen first-hand how destructive the use of drugs may be tempted to try if drugs and drug paraphernalia are within easy reach.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Under the new measures, parents or guardians of youth abusers will be required to undergo mandatory counselling sessions.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: However, siblings of these young drug abusers need to be counselled, too, to explain to them the ills of drug abuse and what might have pushed their sibling to consume illegal drugs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This could go some way to help prevent the siblings from turning to drug abuse as well.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It is important that we let these youths understand the ills of the misuse of drugs.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: CNB can work with SCORE to use these counselling sessions to teach them on how to rehabilitate their family member back into society upon release.

speaker: Mr Melvin Yong Yik Chye (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Let us continue our stand of zero-tolerance on drug abuse and do more to stop the rise of first-time drug abusers and intergenerational addiction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Many of them strongly support Singapore's comprehensive anti-drug strategy.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The amendments to the MDA are significant and I would like to, first, touch on the areas which relate to how we are better protecting our children and youths from the dangers of drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Members have shown strong support for the creation of new offences relating to the exposure of children to drugs and permitting young persons to consume drugs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza has reminded us about the episodes which happened last year, where a one-year-old boy was rescued from suspected drug traffickers after his caregiver left him in their care; where a four-year-old girl was discovered with her mother, with sachets of methamphetamine; and a three-month-old girl found in a unit with a suspected drug trafficker and drug abuser and preliminary investigations showed that "ice" was abused during pregnancy and after the child was born.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We need to move quickly to protect our children and prevent tragedies from happening.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Dr Intan Mokhtar asked whether aside from the abuser, other adults in the household will be implicated if drugs are found within a child's access in the home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked why we have decided to take this strong stance, given the alternatives and tradeoffs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In the cases that Mr Christopher de Souza has cited, this is what our officers see on the ground – young children found in drug dens.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They were put in danger, some by their own parents.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Others were passed around among caregivers who were either drug abusers or traffickers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Paraphrasing what Dr Intan Mokhtar said, as adults, we cannot ignore our responsibility towards our children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is a basic baseline safety that must be upheld and children from all backgrounds are deserving of that same protection.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira asked why we decided to create this specific provision in the MDA rather than rely on other Acts.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This is because of the specific trends and issues we have observed in the course of drug enforcement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The provisions in the CYPA, for instance, require that the offender has a custodial relationship with the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Whereas in the cases we see, there are scenarios, such as a parent leaving his child at a friend's house.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The friend then abuses drugs, and the child is exposed to the drugs left openly around.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under CYPA, the friend may not be liable, having no relationship with the child, even though his behaviour has put the child in danger.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The MDA, hence, provides specifically for such permutations of scenarios on the ground and the punishments correspondingly reflect the great capacity for harm that drugs can have, especially on children.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira has valid concerns about how this ultimately works towards the welfare of the child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The purpose of section 11B is, first and foremost, for deterrence, as we do not wish to see innocent children harmed because of the bad choices others make.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Nevertheless, please rest assured that our enforcement agencies will also work together with the AGC, MSF and other relevant authorities to assess how to best safeguard the family's welfare.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: That said, we are concerned about older youths as well and, as Mr Melvin Yong observed, more liberal attitudes, combined with easy access to drugs, mean that they may be more likely to give in.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hence, there is also a section 11(B)(2), which makes it an offence for an adult who permits, or does not take reasonable steps to prevent, a young person under 21 from consuming illicit drugs in the adult's possession.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As Mr Faisal Manap has mentioned, education about these offences is important and raising general awareness will help deter such irresponsible actions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will continue to educate all members of the public through our various preventive drug education platforms.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Next, to support youth drug abusers and get them to turn over a new leaf, the support of their parents and guardians is critical.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the topic of compulsory counselling for parents/guardians of youth drug abusers who are under CNB's supervision order, Ms Anthea Ong and Dr Intan Mokhtar have asked for further details.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It will differ for each abuser and this is calibrated to the abuser's and his family's specific needs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Some sessions will involve only the youth abuser, some only the parents, and others are joint sessions.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hence, the rehabilitation process must have the flexibility to cater to the unique circumstances and needs of these different families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Sometimes, the counsellors need to counsel the parents privately, to address complex issues affecting their child.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As the Minister mentioned earlier, parents/guardians today are already required to attend the counselling sessions, just that some persistently absent themselves.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Hence, we have now made clear in the MDA that they have a legal responsibility to attend counselling, which is key to supporting their child's or ward's rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Failure to do so will be an offence and we intend for this to come into force by the first half of this year.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Dr Chia Shi-Lu and Mr Desmond Choo had asked whether the focus on rehabilitation and the perceived lack of penalties may encourage more young abusers to experiment.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We want to intervene early and effectively, to allow them to continue to study and be with their families where possible.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For youth abusers under 21, we have the Youth Enhanced Supervision for low-risk abusers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have the Community Rehabilitation Centre for moderate-risk abusers and we have the DRC for high-risk abusers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: So, it is not that experimentation with drugs is cost-free for the young.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: I also want to emphasise that we are not becoming more permissive about drugs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Drugs come at a high cost to society, and suffering behind every abuser is a family.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We have no reason to go soft, and we must not.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: What we are doing is keeping abreast of new research and developments, to inform and refine our approach, to help us better achieve our aim of reducing overall drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Even as we undertake these new initiatives to better protect our children and youths, we must guard against individuals who undertake contaminated practices to spread the use of drugs and cause others to abuse drugs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: They can harm not only our young but also others.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: On the introduction of contamination offences, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah asked whether someone replying to another person's question about manufacturing drugs constitutes a contamination offence.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: This will depend on the context in which the question is asked, and also the answer given.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is also not intended to target the provision of information for legitimate purposes or licensed activities, for example, staff in a pharmaceutical company licensed to manufacture medication, providing information to one another as part of the manufacturing process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Minister has explained earlier that we have provided for defences in the Act, and the subsidiary legislation will set out the scope of authorised activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is also a lot of information on the Internet on carrying out drug activities.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: While we cannot police the whole Internet, if a person in Singapore disseminates or publishes such information online, without any legitimate purpose, he can be investigated for an offence under section 11(D)(2).

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We are now building upon the success of past efforts in addressing reoffending.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Taskforce on Drugs was formed in October 2011.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Chaired by then-Minister of State for Home Affairs and Foreign Affairs Mr Masagos Zulkifli, one of the key recommendations was the implementation of a structured aftercare regime with more scaffolding for offenders, tighter supervision and enhanced community support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The Mandatory Aftercare Scheme (MAS) was piloted in 2012 and operationalised in July 2014.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Under MAS, higher-risk offenders, including LT inmates, go through structured stepdown interventions like compulsory counselling, case management and supervision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It has only been a few years since MAS was implemented but the results are encouraging.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Ex-inmates have also provided feedback that having counsellors and officers walk with them in their reintegration journey has helped them stay accountable and provided them with a source of support when they struggle with life outside.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Desmond Choo asked whether the DRC length is too short and Er Dr Lee Bee Wah also asked how we determine when a person no longer requires supervision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: CNB and SPS track the person throughout his detention and the CBP phase as well as the supervision phase.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: What Mr Desmond Choo mentioned are rough indicative ranges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But each individual is different, so their own risk and progress will determine the length of each phase.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Regular reviews are done to assess rehabilitation progress.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As he shows improvement and stays clean, he can be considered for progressively lower frequencies of urine/hair testing until he is assessed suitable for release from his supervision.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The journey is difficult and, ultimately, the ability of the person to stay clean depends on his own resolve.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we are doing more to provide support where we can.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: In that respect, Mr Pritam Singh, Mr Murali Pillai, Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Ms Joan Pereira have asked whether there are adequate support and training for counsellors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: All of SPS' correctional rehabilitation specialists possess qualifications in relevant disciplines, and SPS also provides on-the-job training.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: It is a very meaningful, rewarding but challenging calling.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Thus, there are also senior staff there to provide guidance and help them avoid burnout.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: SPS also has an inhouse team of psychologists that they can turn to for mental or emotional support.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: SPS also collaborated with the Social Service Institute to introduce training modules last year that will help build up the capabilities of case managers and counsellors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: As several Members have noted, all these rehabilitation initiatives can be resource-intensive.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we use digital technology to help, where possible, and the app and video-conferencing initiatives mentioned by Mr Mohamed Irshad will go a long way to benefiting inmates, including drug offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Christopher de Souza and Mr Louis Ng provided other good suggestions for inmates, such as having more open visits, providing them with more workbooks and healthy physical activities, and providing them with more support during the initial incarceration phase.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are some of the good practices SPS has already put in place and they will continue to work on them.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Mr Melvin Yong also spoke about early interventions for abusers’ families.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We will also continue working with community partners to ensure that abusers’ children who are at-risk are referred to the proper channels for assistance and counselling where required.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Deputy Speaker, the amendments to the MDA are significant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: There is a sizeable section in the amendments that is devoted to protecting our children and our youths from drug abuse.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The examples Mr Christopher de Souza brought up earlier in his speech are shocking, sad and true.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We cannot allow them to have their lives ruined just because of the bad choices adults make with regard to drugs, or their irresponsible behaviour, for example, leaving their children in the care of caregivers who are drug abusers or drug traffickers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Family support is important in our rehabilitation efforts for drug abusers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: For inmates, SPS will continue to work with families and also MSF to identify the needs of their families, provide intervention and increase family involvement in inmate rehabilitation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: Members Er Dr Lee Bee Wah and Mr Pritam Singh have highlighted the importance of ensuring adequate resources for the counsellors and also their psychological well-being.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: These are the important points which I have highlighted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: But we must also guard against the external influences which propagate the use of drugs and help those who have been negatively influenced to prevent more people from taking drugs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: The introduction of contamination offences moves to stem this.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: We share Member Er Dr Lee Bee Wah's concerns about the availability of information on drugs online.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: And that is why Singapore has a comprehensive harm prevention strategy against drugs where preventive drug education is our first line of defence, then coupled with tough laws and vigorous enforcement against drug traffickers, and structured rehabilitation and supervision to help abusers kick the drug habit.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Home Affairs (Ms Sun Xueling)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, my colleague, Senior Parliamentary Secretary Amrin Amin, will now be addressing some of the other issues that Members have raised.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The first, the mandatory minimum sentence for drug consumption; second, hair analysis; third, international cooperation in cross-border drug enforcement; and fourth, cannabis and our preventive drug education.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Drug addiction is a complex issue, as what Ms Anthea Ong has noted.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: It is a confluence of biological, psychological and social factors, and we adopt a multi-pronged approach to tackling drug addiction.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Robust laws, a fair criminal justice system, evidence-based rehabilitation framework, community and family support, all play an important part.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Pritam Singh asked about how many of the DRC inmates are first-timers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Pritam Singh has also asked for family and income profile of DRC inmates.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We do not have the information currently, and may I invite the Member to file a separate Parliamentary Question on this?

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The key challenge is to ensure that our people do not even start on drugs and get entangled in this complex issue.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Murali Pillai, Mr Louis Ng and Ms Anthea Ong have asked what the policy consideration to impose the mandatory minimum sentence for drug consumption was.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: This is a deliberate policy decision by the Government.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The Courts still retain discretion in the following ways: sentencing above the prescribed one year, that is, the Court can impose a sentence from one to a maximum of 10 years; and when a person is also charged with other criminal charges, the Court retains the discretion to order the drug consumption sentence to run concurrently or consecutively with that of the other charges.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: The mandatory minimum sentence has to be seen against the larger context of the rehabilitative framework for drug abusers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We have introduced various calibrated rehabilitative programmes for both youth and adult drug abusers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: These programmes cater to the different circumstances and risk levels of the individual abuser.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: So, the reality today is that not all offences of consumption are treated the same.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: There is no rigid, immutable starting point as an offender can be directed to the newly introduced EDSO or DRC, and, for youths, Youth Enhanced Supervision, Community Rehabilitation Centre (DRC) and, as the Minister earlier said, we are also introducing a surrender regime.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: So, the programmes are varied and tailored to the need of the offenders.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Given the many varied and expanded options, the mandatory minimum sentence for drug consumption is important in maintaining the Government’s firm stance against drugs.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: On hair analysis, Mr Christopher de Souza has asked how often a person needs to report for hair testing.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Hair testing will complement urine testing and, generally, the abuser will need to report to CNB once every month.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Mr Mohamed Irshad and Mr Faisal Manap have also provided some feedback on the supervision process.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We are aware of this and are monitoring closely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: We will see how we can leverage technology, like hair analysis, which could reduce the frequency of reporting.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: Ms Joan Pereira asked about border security and how we work with other organisations to keep drugs out of Singapore.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
text: In particular, she has asked about checks at our checkpoints.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home Affairs (Mr Amrin Amin)
